module.title: Foundations of Food Allergens
module.description: Foundations of food allergens: what a food allergy is, the FDA Top 9 allergens, and allergic reactions and anaphylaxis.

lessons.title: What Is a Food Allergy?
lessons.body_md:
A food allergy is an immune system reaction to a food protein. Unlike food preferences or intolerances, allergic reactions can become serious and life-threatening.

Even a small amount of an allergen can trigger a reaction in sensitive individuals.

Restaurants must take all allergy disclosures seriously.

This training is designed to help restaurants reduce allergen risk through education, communication, and structured procedures.

No restaurant can guarantee a completely allergen-free environment. The goal of this program is to improve awareness, reduce preventable mistakes, and support safer food handling practices.

## Key Concepts

- Food allergies involve the immune system
- Small amounts of allergens can trigger reactions
- Allergic reactions can become severe quickly
- Restaurants should focus on risk reduction, not guarantees
- Honest communication is critical

lessons.title: Understanding the Top 9 Food Allergens
lessons.body_md:
The FDA identifies 9 major food allergens responsible for the majority of serious allergic reactions in the United States.

Every restaurant staff member should be familiar with these allergens.

1. **Milk (Dairy)** — Milk is found in cheese, butter, cream sauces, soups, dressings, and many prepared foods.

   Common restaurant examples include:
   - Alfredo sauce
   - Ranch dressing
   - Mashed potatoes
   - Cream soups
   - Cheese blends
2. **Eggs** — Eggs are commonly used in baking, sauces, breading, desserts, and pasta.

   Common restaurant examples include:
   - Mayonnaise
   - Aioli
   - Pancake batter
   - Fried food breading
   - Desserts
3. **Peanuts** — Peanuts are a separate allergen from tree nuts and may appear in oils, sauces, desserts, and Asian dishes.

   Common restaurant examples include:
   - Peanut oil
   - Peanut sauces
   - Dessert toppings
   - Asian marinades
4. **Tree Nuts** — Tree nuts include almonds, walnuts, cashews, pecans, pistachios, and more.

   Common restaurant examples include:
   - Pesto
   - Nut garnishes
   - Desserts
   - Nut oils
5. **Soy** — Soy is commonly found in sauces, marinades, dressings, and processed foods.

   Common restaurant examples include:
   - Soy sauce
   - Teriyaki sauce
   - Marinades
   - Dressings
6. **Wheat** — Wheat is a grain found in bread, pasta, breading, flour, and many sauces.

   Common restaurant examples include:
   - Bread
   - Pasta
   - Roux
   - Fried food breading
   - Soy sauce
7. **Fish** — Fish includes finned fish such as salmon, tuna, cod, and others.

   Common restaurant examples include:
   - Fish sauce
   - Caesar dressing
   - Seafood dishes
   - Stocks
8. **Shellfish** — Shellfish includes shrimp, crab, lobster, clams, scallops, and oysters.

   Common restaurant examples include:
   - Shrimp dishes
   - Oyster sauce
   - Seafood stock
   - Crab mixtures
9. **Sesame** — Sesame is increasingly common in restaurant foods.

   Common restaurant examples include:
   - Tahini
   - Sesame oil
   - Burger buns
   - Dressings
   - Asian sauces

> **Important:**
> Allergens may not always be visible or obvious.
>
> Staff should never guess whether a dish is safe.
>
> Ingredients must always be verified.

lessons.title: Understanding Allergic Reactions and Anaphylaxis
lessons.body_md:
Allergic reactions can range from mild symptoms to severe, life-threatening emergencies.

A severe allergic reaction is called anaphylaxis.

Anaphylaxis can happen quickly and requires immediate action.

Common symptoms may include:

- Hives or rash
- Swelling of the lips, face, or throat
- Difficulty breathing
- Wheezing
- Vomiting
- Dizziness or fainting
- Tightness in the chest

Restaurants should always take allergic reactions seriously.

If a severe reaction is suspected:

- Alert a manager immediately
- Call 911
- Stay with the guest
- Never assume symptoms will improve on their own

## Key Concepts

- Allergic reactions can escalate quickly
- Immediate action matters
- Staff should never ignore symptoms
- Emergency response awareness is critical
